modules.title: Sales Operations & Sales Intelligence

lesson.title: From sales data to action
lesson.summary: Trace the sales intelligence journey from raw data to decisions.
objectives: Define sales intelligence and the sales operations role
Map the full sales lifecycle from lead to closed deal
Identify the key metrics that run a sales funnel
Explain descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics
lesson.content:
Sales intelligence is the practice of turning reliable CRM and activity data into decisions that help sales teams prioritise action. A sales operations or sales intelligence professional is the person who builds the reporting, processes and data standards that let the whole team see what is working and what is not. Before any dashboard, scoring model or AI workflow makes sense, you need to understand the journey every potential customer takes.

## The sales organisation

A modern B2B sales team runs on a set of standard objects. A lead is anyone who might become a customer. An MQL (marketing-qualified lead) meets marketing-fit criteria. An SQL (sales-qualified lead) has been checked by sales and confirmed as worth pursuing. An opportunity is a real deal being worked, a proposal is pricing shared, and a closed-won or closed-lost outcome records the final result. Around these sit accounts, contacts, deals and the pipeline — the sum of every active opportunity.

- Lead — a potential customer, not yet qualified
- MQL — qualified by marketing criteria
- SQL — qualified by sales fit and intent
- Opportunity — an active deal with value attached
- Proposal — pricing and terms shared with the buyer
- Closed Won / Closed Lost — the final outcome

## The sales lifecycle

The lifecycle is the sequence every lead moves through. It exists so that work is coordinated: marketing fills the top, sales qualifies and advances, and the CRM records every step so nothing is lost.

- Lead creation
- Qualification (marketing and sales)
- Assignment to an owner
- First contact
- Discovery of needs and budget
- Proposal
- Negotiation
- Closed Won or Closed Lost

Each transition is an opportunity to measure. How many leads become MQLs? How long does an SQL wait for first contact? Which stage loses the most deals? These questions are the raw material of sales intelligence.

## Key sales metrics

The core metrics of a sales funnel are lead volume, conversion rates between stages, pipeline value, win rate, average deal size and sales cycle length. Two operational measures deserve special attention: TAT (turnaround time), which is how quickly the team makes first contact, and stale leads, which are leads that have gone quiet and are at risk of being lost.

- Lead volume — how many enter the top of the funnel
- Conversion rate — percentage advancing between stages
- Lead-to-opportunity — the efficiency of qualification
- Opportunity-to-deal — the efficiency of closing
- Win rate — won deals divided by all decided deals
- Pipeline value — value of open opportunities and proposals
- Average deal size — revenue per won deal
- Sales cycle — average time from lead to close
- TAT — time from creation to first contact
- Stale leads — leads with no recent activity
- Follow-up compliance — whether next actions are actually done

## The analytics ladder

Sales intelligence is not a single report; it is a hierarchy of thinking. Descriptive analytics answers 'what happened' — last month's leads and revenue. Diagnostic analytics answers 'why' — conversion dropped because first contact took too long. Predictive thinking uses patterns to anticipate what happens next, and prescriptive recommendations suggest what to do about it. A great sales intelligence professional moves up this ladder: they report the numbers, explain the causes and recommend the fix.

## Why this matters in this platform

This platform gives you a practice environment: a fictional CRM with leads, stages, scores and activities. The Analytics page is a working example of the reports a sales intelligence professional builds. As you work through the modules, you will clean this data, score and route leads, build dashboards, use AI support and finally assemble everything into a capstone portfolio — a complete sales intelligence system you can show an employer.

## Worked example — reading a funnel

Suppose the fictional NexaFlow data for June shows 120 new leads. By the end of the month, 60 became MQLs, 24 became SQLs, 12 became opportunities, 6 received proposals and 5 closed won.

- Lead to MQL conversion: 60 ÷ 120 = 50%
- MQL to SQL conversion: 24 ÷ 60 = 40%
- SQL to Opportunity: 12 ÷ 24 = 50%
- Opportunity to Proposal: 6 ÷ 12 = 50%
- Proposal to Won: 5 ÷ 6 = 83%

The sharpest drop is MQL to SQL — 40% of MQLs are lost during qualification. A sales intelligence analyst would diagnose this with TAT: if SQLs wait 8 days for first contact while MQLs are contacted in 2, the fix is a faster sales handoff, not more leads at the top. The funnel does not just show the problem; it points to where to look next.

## Practice questions

- Q1: A lead has been checked by marketing but not yet by sales. Which stage is it in?
- Q2: Revenue from won deals divided by all decided deals is which metric?
- Q3: A report says 'conversion dropped because first-contact TAT doubled'. Which level of the analytics ladder is this?
- Q4: List the four levels of the analytics ladder in order.
- Q5: Why does the CRM record every stage transition and not just the final outcome?

### Check your answers

- A1: MQL — it fits marketing criteria but has not been sales-qualified.
- A2: Win rate.
- A3: Diagnostic analytics — it explains why something happened.
- A4: Descriptive, then diagnostic, then predictive, then prescriptive.
- A5: So conversion, TAT and drop-off can be measured at every stage, not only at the end.

files.description: One-line definitions of the 11 core funnel metrics.
files.content:
# Sales Metrics Glossary — NexaFlow Training

| Metric | Definition | Why it matters |
| Lead volume | Leads created in a period | Shows pipeline health at the top of the funnel |
| Conversion rate | % of leads advancing between two stages | Finds the bottleneck in the funnel |
| Lead-to-opportunity | % of leads that become opportunities | Measures qualification efficiency |
| Opportunity-to-deal | % of opportunities that close won | Measures closing efficiency |
| Win rate | Won ÷ (won + lost) | How often the team wins decided deals |
| Pipeline value | Sum of open opportunities and proposals | Revenue in motion |
| Average deal size | Revenue ÷ number of won deals | Pricing and deal-quality signal |
| Sales cycle | Average days from lead to close | Predictability of the process |
| TAT (turnaround time) | Days from lead creation to first contact | Long TAT kills deals |
| Stale leads | Leads with no activity for 7+ days | Deals at risk of going cold |
| Follow-up compliance | % of next actions completed on time | Whether the team does what it commits to|

# Sales Intelligence — Reading Guide

Follow-up reading for Module 1, curated by your instructor.

## 1. Funnel mechanics
- Write out the eight lifecycle steps from the lesson from memory, then check against the content.
- For each step, note the metric that tells you it is working (e.g. lead-to-MQL conversion for qualification).

## 2. TAT and stale leads
- Open the Analytics page and find one lead in the 'At risk' stale bucket, then use its stage history to work out why it went cold.

## 3. From reporting to action
- Pick one dashboard metric and write a 'so what / now what' paragraph: what the number means and the single action it suggests.

## Suggested practice
- Rebuild the funnel calculation from the worked example by hand using the sample lead export (nexaflow-leads-sample.csv).

modules.title: Excel for Sales Intelligence
modules.summary: Prepare and explore sales data in spreadsheets.

lesson.title: Clean data for analysis
lesson.summary: Recognise common data-quality issues before reporting.
objectives: Identify duplicates, missing values and inconsistent fields
Use tables, sorting, filtering and data validation
Apply COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, XLOOKUP and IFERROR to sales data
Build pivot tables for salesperson, source and industry analysis
lesson.content:
Almost every sales analytics failure starts with dirty data. Duplicate leads double-count revenue, missing owners make accountability impossible, and free-text fields such as Source create dozens of variations of the same value. Before you report, you clean — and cleaning is a repeatable skill, not an afterthought. This lesson gives you the exact spreadsheet toolkit a sales operations analyst uses every day.

## The four data-quality problems

When you open a CRM export, you are almost guaranteed to find four issues. Learn to spot each one quickly:

- Duplicate records — the same company or contact appears twice under slightly different names
- Missing values — empty owners, empty sources, missing deal values
- Invalid values — statuses that are not on the approved list, negative revenue, impossible dates
- Inconsistent values — 'Webinar', 'webinar', 'Webinar ' for the same source

A clean dataset answers every question consistently. A dirty one produces a different answer depending on who is asking.

## Excel fundamentals for analysts

Start with the mechanics. Convert your dataset into an Excel table so filters and formulas stay consistent as rows are added. Use sorting and filtering to spot outliers, conditional formatting to highlight missing cells and empty owners, and data validation to force future entries into a fixed value list. Named ranges make your formulas readable when the workbook grows.

- Tables — automatic filtering, consistent ranges
- Sorting and filtering — find outliers fast
- Conditional formatting — highlight missing or unusual values
- Data validation — force entries onto a fixed list
- Named ranges — readable formulas

## The formulas that matter

The essential formulas for sales work are COUNTIFS and SUMIFS for filtered counts and totals, XLOOKUP to join data such as salesperson names to lead IDs, IFERROR to keep formulas from breaking on missing values, and NETWORKDAYS or simple date differences to measure TAT. These cover the majority of sales reporting tasks you will meet.

- SUMIFS — total value of leads from a specific source
- COUNTIFS — count of stale leads per owner
- XLOOKUP — bring company industry into a lead list
- IFERROR — return a blank instead of breaking
- TEXT — format dates and values consistently
- TODAY and NETWORKDAYS — age and TAT calculations

Example: to count how many leads owner 'Taylor Shah' owns that are still open, you write `=COUNTIFS(owner_range, "Taylor Shah", status_range, "Open")`. The same pattern extends to every slice of the business.

## Pivot tables

Pivot tables turn the same worksheet into answers: leads and revenue by salesperson, by source, by industry, by employee size and by campaign. A pivot table is the fastest way to see which rep converts best, which source produces the most pipeline and which industry has the longest cycle. Drag the dimension into Rows, the measure into Values, and the analysis writes itself.

## Putting it together

In the labs you will apply this to a 5,000-row CRM dataset: clean it, calculate lead TAT, identify stale leads, build a funnel analysis and create a salesperson performance report. In this platform, the CRM Lab and Analytics pages give you the same raw material — export the CSV and practise the spreadsheet skills on the fictional NexaFlow data.

## Worked example — cleaning a real export

A CRM export contains 50 rows. Scanning it you find: 'Acme Corp' appears twice under slightly different names, the Source column contains 'Webinar', 'webinar ' and 'Webinar', three rows have no owner, and one deal shows revenue of −500.

- Step 1 — remove exact duplicates by company and contact, keeping the newest record.
- Step 2 — standardise Source with a find-and-replace so 'Webinar' is the only spelling.
- Step 3 — flag the missing owners and route them to the team lead instead of inventing an owner.
- Step 4 — reject the negative revenue row or correct it against the source system.

After cleaning, the same pivot table that previously showed six sources now shows three, and the lead count drops from 50 to 46. The numbers are smaller and correct — that is the point. A formula check: `=COUNTIFS(source_range, "Webinar")` now counts every webinar lead exactly once.

## Practice questions

- Q1: Why is 'Webinar', 'webinar' and 'Webinar ' the most dangerous of the four data-quality problems?
- Q2: Which formula counts leads per owner without writing a filter first?
- Q3: Which formula keeps a lookup from showing #N/A when a match is missing?
- Q4: A pivot table shows 12 'sources' but the business only has 6. What is the likely cause?
- Q5: Should you invent an owner for a lead with a missing owner field? Why or why not?

### Check your answers

- A1: Because it is invisible — the data looks fine, but every count, pivot and dashboard built on it is wrong.
- A2: COUNTIFS — for example `=COUNTIFS(owner_range, "Taylor Shah")`.
- A3: IFERROR — for example `=IFERROR(XLOOKUP(...), "")`.
- A4: Inconsistent free-text values — spelling, case or trailing spaces — creating phantom sources.
- A5: No — inventing data destroys trust; flag it and fix the process that allowed it.

files.name: excel-formula-cheatsheet.md
files.label: Excel formula cheat sheet (Markdown)
files.description: COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, XLOOKUP, IFERROR and date formulas with examples.
files.content:
# Excel Formula Cheat Sheet — Sales Intelligence

## Counting and totals
- `=COUNTIF(range, "Webinar")` — count cells equal to a value
- `=COUNTIFS(owner_range, "Jordan Lee", stage_range, "Open")` — count with multiple criteria
- `=SUMIFS(value_range, source_range, "Webinar")` — total value for one source
- `=SUMIFS(value_range, source_range, "Webinar", owner_range, "Jordan Lee")` — total value for a source and owner

## Lookups and joins
- `=XLOOKUP(lead_id, lead_id_range, owner_range)` — bring a value from another table
- `=XLOOKUP(company_id, company_id_range, industry_range, "Not found")` — with a fallback
- `=IFERROR(XLOOKUP(...), "")` — return a blank instead of #N/A

## Dates and TAT
- `=TODAY()` — current date
- `=NETWORKDAYS(created_date, first_contact_date)` — working days between two dates
- `=ROUND((first_contact_date - created_date) * 1.0, 1)` — calendar-day TAT as a number

## Cleaning
- `=TRIM(A2)` — remove trailing spaces
- `=UPPER(A2)` / `=LOWER(A2)` — normalise case
- `=IF(COUNTIF($A$2:$A2, A2) > 1, "DUPLICATE", "")` — flag duplicates
- `=IF(ISBLANK(B2), "MISSING", B2)` — flag missing values

## Example task
Total pipeline value for Webinar leads owned by Jordan Lee:
`=SUMIFS(value_range, source_range, "Webinar", owner_range, "Jordan Lee")`

modules.title: Power BI Sales Dashboard Mastery
modules.summary: Turn sales data into a management dashboard.

lesson.title: Define sales KPIs
lesson.summary: Use clear KPI definitions before building a dashboard.
objectives: Define KPIs with a formula everyone agrees on
Build an executive, funnel, TAT and stale-lead dashboard
Connect data with a clean data model
Read a dashboard as management would
lesson.content:
A dashboard is only as good as its KPI definitions. If two people interpret 'pipeline value' differently, the dashboard creates arguments instead of clarity. So the first step of any Power BI project is writing down what each measure means and how it is calculated: total leads, MQL, SQL, opportunities, proposals, won deals, pipeline value, revenue and win rate.

## KPI definitions first

Every measure needs a written definition with a formula. For example:

- Win rate = closed-won deals divided by (closed-won + closed-lost) deals
- Pipeline value = sum of value of all open opportunities and proposals
- TAT = average days from lead creation to first logged activity or stage movement

Write these down before you open Power BI. A KPI without a definition is a debate waiting to happen.

## The executive dashboard

The executive dashboard answers 'how is the business doing right now' with headline KPIs: total leads, MQL, SQL, opportunities, proposals, won deals, pipeline value, win rate and revenue. It is a health check, not a deep dive — management wants the current state at a glance and the ability to drill into what changed.

## The funnel dashboard

The funnel dashboard shows the lifecycle as a narrowing shape: leads to MQL to SQL to opportunity to proposal to won. The value of a funnel is that it shows exactly where conversion drops off. If 100 leads become 60 MQLs but only 10 become SQLs, qualification is the bottleneck — and the funnel says so visually.

- Leads
- MQL
- SQL
- Opportunity
- Proposal
- Won

## TAT and stale-lead dashboards

The TAT dashboard tracks how quickly the team makes first contact, both on average and by salesperson and stage. The stale-lead dashboard lists leads that have had no activity for 7, 15 or 30+ days so nothing goes cold unnoticed. These two reports are where operational discipline shows up in the numbers.

## The data model

Behind the visuals sits a data model. Power Query cleans and shapes the imported Excel or CRM data, and relationships connect leads, companies, salespeople and opportunities so a single filter updates every visual consistently. Getting the model right matters more than the chart types you choose.

## Your reference implementation

The Analytics page in this platform is a working example of these exact reports: KPI cards, a funnel, breakdowns by salesperson and source, TAT and stale-lead reports with period filters and CSV export. Use it as your reference while you rebuild the same logic in Power BI for the capstone.

## Worked example — writing definitions before the dashboard

The leadership team asks for 'pipeline'. Before opening Power BI, you write the definition: pipeline value = sum of amount for all open opportunities and proposals, excluding closed-won and closed-lost. You also define win rate = won ÷ (won + lost) and TAT = average days from lead creation to first logged activity.

With definitions agreed, the numbers become unambiguous. If pipeline is $400k under your definition but a salesperson counts $520k because they include closed-won deals, the definition settles the disagreement — closed deals are revenue, not pipeline. The dashboard then shows KPI cards (pipeline $400k, win rate 50%, TAT 4.2 days), a funnel with conversion labels between every pair of stages, and a stale-lead table. Anyone can audit any number back to the definition, which is what makes the dashboard a management tool rather than a decoration.

## Practice questions

- Q1: Why must win rate be defined as won ÷ (won + lost) rather than won ÷ all leads?
- Q2: Which dashboard answers 'where is the funnel losing deals'?
- Q3: What does the TAT dashboard measure per salesperson?
- Q4: Why does the data model matter more than the chart type you choose?
- Q5: Name the four dashboards a sales intelligence function typically maintains.

### Check your answers

- A1: Because the denominator is decided deals — leads still open have not lost anything.
- A2: The funnel dashboard, which shows conversion between each pair of stages.
- A3: Average time from lead creation to first contact, so slow reps are visible.
- A4: A clean model makes every visual consistent; a wrong relationship makes charts contradict each other.
- A5: Executive (KPI), funnel, TAT and stale-lead dashboards.

files.content:
# KPI Definitions — Sales Intelligence Dashboard

Every measure must be written down before the dashboard is built. Agree on the formula, then build the visual.

## Core measures
| KPI | Definition | Formula |
| Lead volume | Leads created in the period | COUNT of leads |
| MQL | Marketing-qualified leads | COUNT where stage = MQL or later |
| SQL | Sales-qualified leads | COUNT where stage = SQL or later |
| Opportunity | Active deals | COUNT where stage = OPPORTUNITY or later |
| Proposal | Pricing shared | COUNT where stage = PROPOSAL |
| Won deals | Closed wins | COUNT where stage = CLOSED_WON |
| Pipeline value | Value of open deals | SUM(amount) where stage IN (OPPORTUNITY, PROPOSAL) |
| Revenue | Closed-won value | SUM(amount) where stage = CLOSED_WON |
| Win rate | Won ÷ decided | COUNT(CLOSED_WON) ÷ COUNT(CLOSED_WON + CLOSED_LOST) |
| TAT | First-contact speed | AVG(days from lead creation to first activity or stage move) |
| Stale leads | No recent activity | COUNT where last activity is older than the threshold |

## The four dashboards
1. Executive — headline KPIs for leadership
2. Funnel — conversion between every pair of stages
3. TAT — first-contact speed by rep and by stage
4. Stale — leads needing attention, by bucket

## Data model notes
- Leads join to Companies on company_id
- Leads join to Salespeople on owner_id
- Opportunities join to Leads on lead_id
- One filter updates every visual only if the relationships are correct

modules.title: CRM Fundamentals & Governance
modules.summary: Design reliable CRM data and operating rules.

lesson.title: CRM field governance
lesson.summary: Set practical standards for CRM records.
objectives: Describe the lead-to-account-to-opportunity CRM architecture
Define required fields, value lists and validation rules
Explain data ownership and duplicate management
Map business requirements to CRM fields
lesson.content:
A CRM is only as valuable as the records inside it. The architecture is a chain: a lead becomes a contact, the contact belongs to an account, the account carries opportunities, and opportunities close as deals. Every object has fields, and every field needs a standard so that ten people entering data produce ten consistent records instead of ten interpretations.

## CRM architecture

The objects connect in a standard flow. Understanding this flow tells you where each piece of data lives and which table it belongs to.

- Lead — an unqualified potential customer
- Contact — a person, often tied to an account
- Account — a company you do business with
- Opportunity — a deal being worked on an account
- Deal — a won opportunity with a closed value
- Activity — a call, email, meeting or note
- Campaign — a source of leads

## What field governance means

Field governance is the set of rules that keeps data trustworthy. It answers four questions: what is required, what values are allowed, who is accountable, and how do we stop it degrading.

- Required fields — a lead cannot be saved without an owner or a source
- Fixed value lists — Source must be one of Webinar, Inbound, Referral, Partner, Outbound, Content Download
- Validation rules — reject impossible values such as negative revenue
- Duplicate management — a defined merge process for repeated companies or contacts
- User permissions — who can edit, who can only view
- Data ownership — a named person responsible for each record's accuracy

## Field mapping

A simple field-mapping exercise — business requirement to CRM field — makes the standard concrete. When marketing says 'we need to know where leads come from', the answer is a field with a fixed value list.

- Company name maps to Account Name
- Industry maps to Industry
- Employee size maps to Employee Size
- Lead source maps to Lead Source
- Sales owner maps to Lead Owner
- Lead status maps to Lead Status
- Expected value maps to Deal Value

## The governance workflow

Finally, a CRM runs on workflow: new lead, validate, assign, notify the salesperson, follow up, qualify, opportunity. Every step can be automated and every step can be measured. The platform's CRM Lab lets you practise exactly this — create leads, assign owners, move stages and log activities, with every change recorded in stage history. That history is the audit trail that makes governance measurable.

## Worked example — one field, one standard

Marketing asks for a 'campaign' field. Without governance, ten reps enter ten values: 'web', 'Email Blast', 'NFR', 'summer-campaign' — after a month the field is unusable and analytics cannot group it.

The governed answer: add a Lead Source field with a fixed value list (Webinar, Inbound, Referral, Partner, Outbound, Content Download), make it required on create, and add a validation rule that rejects anything not on the list. New leads cannot be saved without a source. Within one quarter every count by source is trustworthy, and the same field feeds the Analytics breakdowns and the lead scoring model — one standard, many uses.

## Practice questions

- Q1: A lead cannot be saved without an owner or a source. Which governance element is this?
- Q2: Why is a fixed value list better than a free-text field for Source?
- Q3: Who owns the accuracy of a lead record?
- Q4: Two company records exist for the same account. What is the governed response?
- Q5: Where does the audit trail of every stage change live in this platform?

### Check your answers

- A1: Required fields, enforced by validation rules.
- A2: It eliminates the invisible inconsistency that breaks counts and dashboards.

- A5: Stage history on each lead — the CRM Lab records every transition with who, when and why.

modules.title: Lead Management & Funnel Optimization
modules.summary: Qualify, route and progress leads consistently.

lesson.title: Lead lifecycle basics
lesson.summary: Use lifecycle stages to coordinate sales action.
objectives: Distinguish MQL and SQL and the handoff between them
Design a lead scoring model with weighted factors
Route leads with assignment rules that respect workload
Measure TAT and manage stale leads
lesson.content:
The funnel only works when every lead moves through a defined lifecycle with clear owners. An MQL fits marketing criteria; sales confirms fit and intent to make it an SQL. That handoff is where leads get lost if nobody owns the transition. A defined lifecycle, with stage history, makes the handoff auditable and prevents records from slipping away.

## Qualification: MQL to SQL

The MQL/SQL distinction is the most important handoff in the funnel. Marketing generates volume; sales confirms quality. An MQL becomes an SQL when a salesperson verifies that the company fits, the contact is a decision-maker or influencer, and there is a real need and budget.

- MQL — fits marketing criteria, worth a sales call
- SQL — sales-confirmed fit and intent, being worked
- Handoff — who owns the transition, and how fast

## Lead scoring

Lead scoring is the discipline of turning judgment into a repeatable number. A typical model adds points for enterprise company size, target industry, decision-maker title, website engagement and a demo request. The total score tells the team who to call first.

- Enterprise company size +20
- Target industry +20
- Decision-maker title +25
- Website engagement +15
- Demo requested +30

Scores should be transparent: anyone should be able to explain why a lead scored 85. In the Workflow Lab you can see the NexaFlow scoring factors, adjust the weights and watch every lead's score recalculate transparently.

## Lead assignment

Scoring decides priority; assignment decides ownership. Assignment rules route leads by geography, industry, company size, product, score and — critically — salesperson workload. A rule that sends every high-score lead to one rep fails if that rep is at capacity, so good routing checks open pipeline against capacity before assigning.

- Geography — region matches territory
- Industry — industry specialisation
- Company size — SMB, mid-market or enterprise
- Score — high-priority leads to senior reps
- Workload — never overload one rep

The platform simulates this and explains the reason behind every suggested assignment.

## TAT and stale leads

Two metrics keep the funnel healthy. TAT measures the time from lead creation to first contact — the longer it is, the more deals die. Stale leads are those with no activity for several days:

- 0–3 days — Normal
- 4–7 days — Attention
- 8–15 days — At risk
- 15+ days — Stale

The Analytics and Workflow pages surface both automatically so you can practise spotting and fixing them before they go cold.

## Worked example — scoring and routing a new lead

A new lead arrives from a partner referral: a 201–500 employee company in the Logistics industry, the contact is an Operations Director, and an activity was logged yesterday. Against the NexaFlow scoring factors:

- Company fit — mid-market (201–500 employees): +20
- Industry fit — Logistics is on the configured target list: +20
- Decision-maker title — Director matches: +25
- Engagement — activity within the last 7 days: +15
- Intent — Partner is a high-intent source: +15
- Stage is NEW, so the 'moved past NEW' factor does not apply: +0

Total score: 95. Routing then evaluates the assignment rules in priority order: the enterprise-size rule does not match, the Europe rule does not match, but the high-score rule (score at least 80) matches and assigns the lead to the senior rep, Jordan Lee. Before the assignment is final, the workload check confirms Jordan has capacity. The lead is assigned with a stored reason — 'Score ≥ 80 → senior rep' — so the routing decision is auditable.

## Practice questions

- Q1: What is the difference between an MQL and an SQL?
- Q2: Why must assignment rules check workload before assigning?
- Q3: A lead scores 60 with a decision-maker title and a target industry. Name one factor that could push it to 80+.
- Q4: A lead has had no activity for 9 days. Which stale bucket is it in?
- Q5: What does TAT measure, and why does it matter?

### Check your answers

- A1: An MQL fits marketing criteria; an SQL has been verified by sales as worth pursuing.
- A2: Otherwise one rep's pipeline overloads and high-value leads go cold waiting.
- A3: Engagement (activity within 7 days, +15) and intent (high-intent source, +15), or company-size points.
- A4: At risk — the buckets are 0–3 normal, 4–7 attention, 8–15 at risk, 15+ stale.
- A5: Time from lead creation to first contact; longer TAT means more deals die before anyone engages.

modules.title: Generative AI for Sales Intelligence
modules.summary: Use AI safely for research and analysis support.

lesson.title: Verify AI-assisted research
lesson.summary: Keep human judgement at the centre of AI outputs.
objectives: Explain how LLMs generate text and why they can hallucinate
Write prompts with role, context, data, task and output format
Use AI for company research, qualification and reporting
Verify AI claims before acting on them
lesson.content:
Generative AI is a force multiplier for sales intelligence — and a source of confident mistakes. Large language models predict plausible text, which means they can produce facts that look real but are wrong, a failure mode called hallucination. The first habit of safe AI use is verification: every claim the model makes about a company, person or market must be checked against a reliable source before it drives a decision.

## How AI works, and why it errs

An LLM is a text-prediction engine. It has no database of facts; it has patterns learned from training data. That means it can be brilliant at summarising and drafting, and equally capable of inventing a job title, a revenue figure or a competitor feature. Three rules keep you safe:

- Treat every output as a draft, not a fact
- Verify numbers and names against official sources
- Never paste confidential customer data into a public AI tool

## The prompt framework

Prompting is a skill. A strong prompt framework is Role + Context + Data + Task + Constraints + Output Format + Examples. Instead of 'research this company', give the model its role as a sales researcher, paste the company context you have, ask for a structured output, and require it to flag anything it is unsure of.

- Role — 'You are a B2B sales researcher'
- Context — the company and why you are researching it
- Data — what you already know
- Task — what you want produced
- Constraints — tone, length, language
- Output format — a table, bullet list, or scorecard
- Examples — one worked example of the output you want

## The highest-value use cases

The strongest uses for sales are research, qualification, follow-up and reporting.

- Company, industry and competitor research
- Lead qualification — score, reason, pain points, suggested questions
- Follow-up drafting — emails, LinkedIn messages, meeting summaries
- Reporting — raw numbers into a management summary with issues and recommended actions

## The human approval gate

None of these should send anything automatically. The AI Practice Lab in this platform simulates all of it without an API key: run the templates, copy the prompts, and practise the human review step. Follow-up drafts are marked approved or sent only by you. That approval gate is not bureaucracy — it is the whole point of responsible AI-assisted sales work.

## Worked example — a prompt, and a hallucination caught

A rep asks a model: 'Write 3 bullet points about BrightForge Manufacturing.' The model returns 'revenue $1.2bn, 4,000 employees, HQ Bangalore'. The numbers are plausible — and wrong: the official record shows a 501–1000 employee manufacturing company in India. The model invented figures because it was asked for facts it had not been given.

The governed version uses the prompt framework and treats output as a draft:

- Role: 'You are a B2B sales researcher for NexaFlow.'
- Context: 'BrightForge Manufacturing is a fictional mid-market company in our training CRM.'
- Task: 'Summarise what the CRM shows, then suggest two open questions for discovery.'
- Constraints: 'Do not invent company facts. If the CRM has no data, say so.'
- Output format: 'Three bullets, then two questions.'

With constraints explicit, the model either uses the data you gave it or flags the gap — and the rep still verifies against the CRM before sending anything.

## Practice questions

- Q1: Why can an LLM confidently state a wrong revenue figure?
- Q2: Name the seven parts of the prompt framework taught in this lesson.
- Q3: Why must follow-up drafts go through an approval step before being sent?
- Q4: Should you paste real customer data into a public AI tool? Why or why not?
- Q5: What is the single habit that makes AI-assisted research safe?

### Check your answers

- A1: It predicts plausible text from patterns; it has no fact database, so plausible is not the same as true.
- A2: Role, context, data, task, constraints, output format and examples.
- A3: Because AI can produce inaccurate or harmful messages; a human must verify before anything is sent.
- A4: No — never paste confidential customer data into a public AI tool.
- A5: Verification — treat every output as a draft and check claims against reliable sources.

files.content:
# AI Prompt Framework — Sales Intelligence

## The seven parts
1. Role — who the model is acting as
2. Context — the situation and why the work is being done
3. Data — what the model is allowed to use
4. Task — what you want produced
5. Constraints — tone, length, language, hard limits
6. Output format — the exact shape of the answer
7. Examples — one worked example of the output

## Template
Role: You are a [role] for [company].
Context: [what is happening, and why].
Data: [facts the model may use; nothing else is allowed].
Task: [produce X].
Constraints: [do not invent facts; flag anything uncertain; length].
Output format: [exact shape of the answer].
Example: [one model answer].

## Worked prompt
Role: You are a B2B sales researcher for NexaFlow.
Context: We are qualifying a lead from the training CRM.
Data: Company = AtlasHR, Industry = Human Resources, Contact = Maya Rivera (VP People Operations), Source = Webinar.
Task: Score the lead 0–100 and give the reason, likely pain points and three discovery questions.
Constraints: Use only the data above. If a fact is missing, say so. Keep it under 150 words.
Output format: Score, reason (one paragraph), pain points (bullets), questions (numbered).

## Safety rules
- Every output is a draft, not a fact
- Verify names and numbers against official sources
- Never paste confidential customer data into a public tool
- Nothing is sent without human approval

# Sample Research Prompt — Company Qualification

Paste this into any LLM, replace the bracketed fields, then verify the output against the CRM before the call.

---
Role: You are a B2B sales researcher for NexaFlow, a workflow automation vendor.
Context: We have a new lead and need a pre-call briefing.
Data: Company: [company name]. Industry: [industry]. Contact: [contact], [job title]. Source: [source]. What we already know from the CRM: [paste lead notes].
Task: Produce a pre-call briefing.
Constraints: Use ONLY the data above plus publicly verifiable facts. Do not invent revenue, headcount or feature claims. Flag anything you are unsure about. Under 200 words.

2. Likely pain points for [job title] (3 bullets)
3. Three discovery questions
4. Anything to verify before the call
---

After the model answers, check every claim against the CRM and the company's public pages. Never send the draft anywhere without human review.

lesson.title: Workflow design
objectives: Identify triggers, conditions and actions in a workflow
Design an AI lead-qualification workflow with a decision branch
Place human approval gates in AI-driven processes
Explain the five core automation use cases for sales operations
lesson.content:
Automation turns repeatable sales work into visible, governed workflows. Every workflow starts with a trigger — the event that begins the process, like a new lead arriving. Conditions decide which path the process takes, and actions do the work: updating a score, sending an alert, creating a task. When you can name the trigger, condition and action of a process, you can automate it.

## The building blocks

Learn the vocabulary of automation before building anything:

- Trigger — the event that starts the workflow
- Condition — a test that decides the path
- Action — work the workflow performs
- Workflow — the complete sequence
- Webhook and API — how systems exchange data
- Human approval — a step where a person must act
- Exception handling — what happens when something fails

## The flagship example: AI lead qualification

The classic sales workflow starts with a new lead and ends with a routed, scored record:

- New lead arrives in the CRM
- The workflow enriches it with company data
- AI drafts a qualification
- A score is written to the record
- A decision branch routes high scores to sales and low scores to a nurture campaign

The Workflow Lab in this platform models this exact logic with the lead-validation, assignment, follow-up and escalation flows.

## The human approval rule

The most important design rule is the human approval gate. When AI drafts a follow-up message, no message should be sent until a person reviews it. In automation terms the workflow stops at an approval step and only continues once the human acts. This is how you keep AI from sending an inaccurate or harmful message.

## The five core use cases

Five automations cover most of sales operations:

- New lead → AI qualification → CRM score
- Stale lead → automatic reminder
- Meeting completed → AI summary → next actions
- Weekly sales data → AI management summary
- Competitor news → AI summary → sales repository

Each one reuses the same building blocks of trigger, condition, action and approval.

## Worked example — mapping the AI lead-qualification workflow

Draw the flow before building it:

- Trigger: a new lead is created in the CRM.
- Step 1 (enrich): the workflow matches the company and attaches industry, employee size and region.
- Step 2 (AI draft): an AI step drafts a qualification — score, reason, pain points and suggested questions.
- Step 3 (write score): the score is written to the lead record.
- Step 4 (branch): if the score is at least 80, route to the senior rep; otherwise route to a nurture campaign.
- Step 5 (approval): any AI-drafted follow-up stops at an approval step and only continues after a human reviews it.

Naming each piece — trigger, condition, action, approval — turns a vague idea into something a no-code tool can build and an auditor can follow. The same five building blocks power the stale-lead reminder and the weekly management summary.

## Practice questions

- Q1: What is the difference between a trigger and a condition?
- Q2: In the flagship workflow, what does the decision branch do with a score under 80?
- Q3: Why does every AI-driven workflow that sends messages need a human approval gate?
- Q4: Name three of the five core sales automation use cases.
- Q5: What should a workflow do when a step fails?

### Check your answers

- A1: A trigger is the event that starts the process; a condition is a test that decides which path it takes.
- A2: It routes the lead to a nurture campaign instead of a sales rep.
- A3: So no inaccurate or harmful AI-generated message is ever sent automatically.
- A4: Any three of: new-lead qualification, stale-lead reminder, meeting summary, weekly management summary, competitor-news briefing.
- A5: Follow the defined exception handling — alert an owner or log the failure so it is never silent.

modules.title: Market & Competitive Intelligence
modules.summary: Create evidence-based market and competitor insight.

lesson.title: Research competitor positioning
objectives: Separate verifiable evidence from opinion
Structure market research with TAM, SAM and SOM
Build battle cards for competitor conversations
Organise a sales enablement repository
lesson.content:
Competitive intelligence is the difference between selling on facts and selling on guesses. Every claim about a competitor — their pricing, positioning, strengths and weaknesses — should trace back to verifiable evidence: their website, pricing page, case studies and public announcements. Rumour and opinion pollute the repository and embarrass the rep who repeats them.

## Evidence over opinion

The golden rule of competitive intelligence: if you cannot cite the source, it does not go in the repository. Compare competitors on the same criteria for every vendor, using public evidence such as pricing pages, product documentation and customer reviews. Never change the criteria to favour one vendor.

- Verifiable evidence only
- Same criteria for every competitor
- Record where each claim came from
- Update regularly — the market changes

## Market research structure

Market research starts with structure. TAM is the total market, SAM the segment you can serve, and SOM the share you can realistically win. Industry trends and customer pain points add the context that makes competitive insight actionable rather than academic.

- TAM — total addressable market
- SAM — serviceable available market
- SOM — serviceable obtainable market
- Trends and pain points — why buyers act
- Industry challenges — what keeps buyers up at night

## Battle cards

The battle card is the practical output. For each competitor, record what they offer, their strengths, their weaknesses, our advantage, the common objection a customer raises, and a suggested response. A good battle card is short, specific and written for the moment of a sales conversation, not a library shelf.

- Competitor and what they offer
- Their strengths
- Their weaknesses
- Our advantage
- Common objection
- Suggested response

## The sales enablement repository

All of this lives in a sales enablement repository — case studies, industry reports, battle cards, scripts, objection handling and conversation starters — kept current and owned by someone. In this platform you will create five fictional competitor profiles for the capstone, with a comparison, battle cards and objection handling, and the Analytics page gives you the industry data to ground your analysis in.

## Worked example — building one battle card from evidence

For the fictional competitor 'FluxDesk' the repository contains: their pricing page (plans from $29 per user per month), their site describing 'workflow automation for mid-market ops teams', and three customer reviews mentioning slow onboarding. Every claim is recorded with its source.

The battle card:

- What they offer: workflow automation for mid-market operations — source: pricing page, retrieved Aug 2026.
- Their strengths: clear self-serve pricing; established brand in ops tools.
- Their weaknesses: reviews cite onboarding taking 4–6 weeks — source: 3 customer reviews, Jul 2026.
- Our advantage: onboarding included and completed in 2 weeks, plus prebuilt NexaFlow templates.
- Common objection: 'FluxDesk is cheaper.'
- Suggested response: 'Their list price is lower, but onboarding runs 4–6 weeks in those reviews; ours is included and done in 2. Here is the comparison.'

The card is short, sourced and written for the moment of the conversation — not a library shelf.

## Practice questions

- Q1: What is the golden rule of competitive intelligence?
- Q2: Define TAM, SAM and SOM in one line each.
- Q3: Why must every competitor be compared on the same criteria?
- Q4: List the six sections of a battle card.
- Q5: A rep suggests adding a rumour a customer told them about a competitor. What do you do?

### Check your answers

- A1: If you cannot cite the source, it does not go in the repository.
- A2: TAM is the whole market, SAM the part you can serve, SOM the share you can realistically win.
- A3: Otherwise the comparison is rigged and the sales team cannot trust it.
- A4: What they offer, strengths, weaknesses, our advantage, common objection, suggested response.
- A5: Refuse it — rumour is not verifiable evidence; keep the repository sourced.

lesson.title: Write a usable SOP
lesson.summary: Make recurring processes clear and accountable.
objectives: Structure an SOP with purpose, inputs, steps, owner and exceptions
Gather requirements from business problem to acceptance criteria
Track issues with owners, priorities and status
Collaborate with sales, marketing, technology, finance and operations
lesson.content:
A standard operating procedure turns tribal knowledge into a process anyone can follow. The useful structure covers why the process exists (purpose), what it needs (inputs), the numbered steps, who is accountable (process owner), and what happens when the standard path does not apply (exception path). An SOP without an owner goes stale; an SOP without exceptions breaks on the first odd case.

## The SOP structure

Every SOP should answer the same five questions. If one is missing, the document is incomplete.

- Purpose — why this process exists
- Inputs — what you need to start
- Steps — the numbered procedure
- Owner — who keeps it current and is accountable
- Exception path — what to do when the standard steps do not fit

## Requirement gathering

The role of a sales operations professional is a bridge between business and technology, so requirement gathering matters as much as writing. The chain runs from business problem to current process to pain point to requirement to solution to acceptance criteria to testing to deployment.

A business requirements document captures the problem, current state, future state, functional requirements, business rules, acceptance criteria, dependencies and risks — so developers and stakeholders agree on what 'done' means.

## Issue management

Issues need the same discipline. An issue tracker with issue, owner, priority, date raised, dependency, status, expected closure and actual closure keeps operational problems from disappearing. In the capstone you will write the seven core SOPs — CRM data entry, lead assignment, lead qualification, stale lead, dashboard usage, AI usage and escalation — each with purpose, owner, steps and version.

## Working with stakeholders

Finally, this work is done with people. Each function cares about different things:

- Sales — velocity and quota
- Marketing — volume and lead quality
- Technology — feasibility and effort
- Finance — cost and return
- Operations — consistency and compliance

Clear requirements and documented processes are how you keep all five aligned.

## Worked example — the lead assignment SOP

Purpose: every new lead gets an owner within 1 working day. Inputs: a validated lead record with company data and score. Steps: (1) score the lead, (2) evaluate assignment rules in priority order, (3) check the matched rep's open workload against capacity, (4) assign and notify, (5) log the rule that fired as the reason. Owner: Sales Operations Manager, reviewed quarterly. Exception path: if the matched rep is at capacity or absent, the lead goes to the on-call rep; if no rule matches, the lead is queued for manual review within 24 hours.

That is a complete, usable SOP — an unfamiliar person could execute it, and a new hire could be trained from it in minutes. The same template produces the other six SOPs: data entry, qualification, stale leads, dashboard usage, AI usage and escalation.

## Practice questions

- Q1: Name the five sections every SOP must have.
- Q2: Why does an SOP need an exception path?
- Q3: What does the requirement chain run from, and to?
- Q4: Which four columns must an issue tracker contain as a minimum?
- Q5: Why does finance care about sales operations requirements?

### Check your answers

- A1: Purpose, inputs, steps, owner and exception path.
- A2: Because real processes always hit cases the standard steps do not cover; without an exception path the process breaks silently.
- A3: From business problem to current process, pain point, requirement, solution, acceptance criteria, testing and deployment.
- A4: Issue, owner, priority and status — plus dates and dependencies when available.
- A5: Because finance owns cost and return — requirements must show the business value of the work.

objectives: List the ten capstone deliverables
Map each deliverable to the platform tools that support it
Plan the implementation work in order
Understand the portfolio and certificate criteria
lesson.content:
The capstone is the point where everything connects. You will build a complete AI-powered sales intelligence and CRM operations system for the fictional NexaFlow company — the same company whose data you have been working with all along — and end with a portfolio that demonstrates a real, working system rather than a folder of notes.

## The ten deliverables

Each deliverable maps to a module and to a tool in this platform:

- Data cleaning — clean the CRM dataset; use the CRM Lab
- CRM data model — design lead, account, opportunity and activity fields
- Lead scoring — build a weighted scoring framework; use the Workflow Lab
- Lead assignment — route leads by rules and workload; use the Workflow Lab
- Sales dashboard — build the KPI, funnel, TAT and stale reports; use Analytics
- AI lead qualification — score, reason, pain points, questions and next action; use the AI Practice Lab
- AI follow-up assistant — the approval-gated follow-up workflow; use the AI Practice Lab
- Competitive intelligence — five profiles, battle cards and objections
- SOP library — the seven core SOPs
- Management report — problem, analysis, insight, recommendation, AI opportunity and impact

## Order matters

Clean the data first, because every later deliverable depends on trustworthy records. Then define the data model, score the leads, build the assignment rules, and only then visualise everything in the dashboard. The AI deliverables sit on top of the same data and workflows, and the management report presents the whole system to an audience that wants a decision, not a demo.

## The portfolio and certificate

Work through the Capstone workspace deliverable by deliverable: read the instructions and rubric, use the related tools linked from each card, submit your work, and respond to feedback until your instructor approves. A certificate is issued once you also reach 80% course completion and a 70% assessment score. When the capstone is approved, your portfolio summary shows every deliverable with its score — the evidence you can show an employer.

## Worked example — a four-week capstone plan

Week 1 — foundation: clean the CRM data (deliverable 1) and design the data model (deliverable 2). Everything later depends on these two. Week 2 — pipeline: build the scoring framework (3) and assignment rules (4) in the Workflow Lab, then assemble the KPI, funnel, TAT and stale dashboards (5) using the Analytics page as reference. Week 3 — AI layer: run the AI lead-qualification (6) and AI follow-up assistant (7) templates in the AI Practice Lab, and build the five competitor profiles with battle cards (8). Week 4 — documentation: write the SOP library (9), compose the management report (10), submit the capstone and respond to instructor feedback.

Each week ends with a checkable output. If week 1 slips, nothing downstream is credible — which is why the order is deliberate and the deliverables build on each other.

## Practice questions

- Q1: List the ten capstone deliverables.
- Q2: Why must data cleaning come before dashboard building?
- Q3: Which platform tools support the scoring and assignment deliverables?
- Q4: What are the three certificate criteria?
- Q5: What does the final portfolio demonstrate to an employer?

### Check your answers

- A1: Data cleaning, CRM data model, lead scoring, lead assignment, sales dashboard, AI lead qualification, AI follow-up assistant, competitive intelligence, SOP library, management report.
- A2: Because every later deliverable — model, scoring, dashboard, AI output — is only as trustworthy as the records it uses.
- A3: The Workflow Lab (scoring factors and assignment rules), with the Analytics page as reference.
- A4: 80% course completion, 70% assessment score and an approved capstone.
- A5: A real, working sales intelligence system — not a folder of notes — built on the fictional NexaFlow data.

# Capstone Plan — AI-Powered Sales Intelligence System

Use this template to plan and track the ten deliverables for the NexaFlow capstone.

## The ten deliverables
1. Data cleaning — clean the CRM dataset (use the CRM Lab and the dirty export)
2. CRM data model — lead, account, opportunity and activity fields
3. Lead scoring — weighted scoring framework (use the Workflow Lab)
4. Lead assignment — rules plus workload routing (use the Workflow Lab)
5. Sales dashboard — KPI, funnel, TAT and stale reports (use Analytics as reference)
6. AI lead qualification — score, reason, pain points, questions (use the AI Practice Lab)
7. AI follow-up assistant — approval-gated follow-ups (use the AI Practice Lab)
8. Competitive intelligence — five profiles, battle cards and objections
9. SOP library — the seven core SOPs
10. Management report — problem, analysis, insight, recommendation, AI opportunity, impact

## Four-week plan
| Week | Focus | Deliverables |
| 1 | Foundation | 1, 2 |
| 2 | Pipeline | 3, 4, 5 |
| 3 | AI layer | 6, 7, 8 |
| 4 | Documentation | 9, 10 |
